# Standard Library Reference

<!-- Generated by scripts/stdlib-reference.mjs --write. Do not edit: change the declarations
     (stdlib/*.cml and stdlib/signatures/*.cml) or the comments of the library and
     regenerate. -->

The functions of the core standard library, by module. The boundary is the one the design
principles draw (section 10.5): a primitive that touches the system or is sensitive to
performance is an operator written in C++, an opaque node of the graph; logic composed from
primitives is written in Camel, a subgraph that passes can see into.

Every function follows the [standard library conventions](stdlib-conventions.cn.md): one fact
one place, the declaration is the signature, naming, parameters, error kinds, and where a
module lives.

How to read an entry:

- **Signature**: `name: <with-parameters> (parameters) => result`. The value a function works
  on is its ordinary parameter and what configures it is a with-parameter, so calls chain:
  `s->trim->split<','>`, `xs->filter<p>->sort_by<key>`. `int` is the 64-bit integer and `float`
  the 64-bit float; `i32` and `f32` are the 32-bit ones; numeric types are never converted
  implicitly.
- **Pure** operators depend on their arguments only: a pass may evaluate a call ahead of time,
  merge two equal calls or drop an unused one. An operator **with effects** is left alone, and
  its call runs only when it is reachable from a `sync` block or its result is used (design
  principles 3.1). Every operator of these modules declares which it is.
- **Failure**: a *fault* stops the program with a located diagnostic (an index out of range, an
  argument outside what the operator defines). An *error* is a value: the function returns
  `T!` and the program handles it with `!!`, `?->` or `match`. A result that may not exist is
  `T?`, handled with `??`. An entry without a failure line does not fail.
- **Named arguments**: a call may give a parameter by name (`f(x: 1)`, `len(x: xs)`) when
  the name gives that position the same name in every form the callee has, whether the callee is
  a Camel declaration or a group of built-in rules; the type of the argument then decides which
  form runs (`len`'s one parameter is `x` for a string, an array, a map and a set, so one name
  reaches all four). The name is written in the list that holds the parameter: an ordinary one
  in the parentheses (`len(x: xs)`), a `with` one in the angle brackets (`j->get<key: 'port'>`).
  A form that gives a position no name, or leaves its count to the arguments (a rest list --
  `py_call`'s two forms differ in arity as well), is one no named argument reaches: the call
  reports that the signature is not known where the call is written. `contains` refuses a named
  argument for a reason of its own: its position 0 means an element in two forms and the
  substring in the third, so the name would mean another thing in one of them.
- Write one call that has with-arguments per statement when several appear in one argument
  list: `f<a>(x), g<b>(y)` is read as comparisons.

Not in this reference: the profiler (`perf`).

## Built-in functions

The operators behind the language's own operators (`+`, `==`, `[]`, `??`, assignment, ...) are
registered under reserved names (`__add__`, ...) and are not listed here.

### Memory

Data blocks (design principles 10.5): the process-wide counters, read between two operations.

#### `std::mem::blocks`

```camel
std::mem::blocks: () => { allocs: int, frees: int, live: int, bytes: int }
```

The data-block counters: blocks allocated so far, freed so far, live now, and the bytes the
live blocks hold. The call is not pure: it reports process state, so the optimizer must not
fold, merge or drop it.

- With effects: reads the process-wide data-block counters.
- Example: `std::mem::blocks().live` gives `0 when no block is alive`

### Conversions

Numeric types are never converted implicitly; these functions do it. Converting a float to
an integer drops the fraction.

#### `int`

```camel
int: (x: i32) => int
int: (x: int) => int
int: (x: f32) => int
int: (x: float) => int
int: (x: string) => int
int: (x: bf16) => int
int: (x: f16) => int
```

x as a 64-bit integer.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidNumberText` when x is a string that is not, as a whole, one integer (blanks and a trailing part included); fault `ConversionOutOfRange` when x is a string that is an integer beyond the range, or a float that is NaN, infinite or beyond the range; use parse_int to handle text in the program.
- Example: `int(2.9)` gives `2`

#### `i64`

```camel
i64: (x: i32) => int
i64: (x: int) => int
i64: (x: f32) => int
i64: (x: float) => int
i64: (x: string) => int
i64: (x: bf16) => int
i64: (x: f16) => int
```

The same as int.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidNumberText` when x is a string that is not, as a whole, one integer; fault `ConversionOutOfRange` when x is a string that is an integer beyond the range, or an int or a float beyond the range of i32, or NaN.
- Example: `i64('42')` gives `42`

#### `i32`

```camel
i32: (x: i32) => i32
i32: (x: int) => i32
i32: (x: f32) => i32
i32: (x: float) => i32
i32: (x: string) => i32
i32: (x: bf16) => i32
i32: (x: f16) => i32
```

x as a 32-bit integer.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidNumberText` when x is a string that is not, as a whole, one integer; fault `ConversionOutOfRange` when x is a string that is an integer beyond the range, or an int or a float beyond the range of i32, or NaN.
- Example: `i32(7)` gives `7`

#### `float`

```camel
float: (x: i32) => float
float: (x: int) => float
float: (x: f32) => float
float: (x: float) => float
float: (x: string) => float
float: (x: bf16) => float
float: (x: f16) => float
```

x as a 64-bit float.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidNumberText` when x is a string that is not, as a whole, one number; fault `ConversionOutOfRange` when x is a string that is a number beyond the range of float (overflow or underflow); use parse_float to handle that in the program.
- Example: `float(3)` gives `3`

#### `f64`

```camel
f64: (x: i32) => float
f64: (x: int) => float
f64: (x: f32) => float
f64: (x: float) => float
f64: (x: string) => float
f64: (x: bf16) => float
f64: (x: f16) => float
```

The same as float.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidNumberText` when x is a string that is not a number; fault `ConversionOutOfRange` when x is a string that is a number beyond the range of float (overflow or underflow).
- Example: `f64('2.5')` gives `2.5`

#### `f32`

```camel
f32: (x: i32) => f32
f32: (x: int) => f32
f32: (x: f32) => f32
f32: (x: float) => f32
f32: (x: string) => f32
f32: (x: bf16) => f32
f32: (x: f16) => f32
```

x as a 32-bit float.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidNumberText` when x is a string that is not a number; fault `ConversionOutOfRange` when x is a string that is a number beyond the range of f32 (overflow or underflow).
- Example: `f32(0.5)` gives `0.5`

#### `bf16`

```camel
bf16: (x: i32) => bf16
bf16: (x: int) => bf16
bf16: (x: f32) => bf16
bf16: (x: float) => bf16
bf16: (x: bf16) => bf16
bf16: (x: string) => bf16
```

x as a bf16: the nearest bf16 of x, rounding to nearest with ties to even, once. A bf16 is a
floating-point type of the language (design principles 7.3), not only a tensor element type,
and writing the conversion asks for that precision, so no numeric permission is involved.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidNumberText` when x is a string that is not a number; fault `ConversionOutOfRange` when x is a string that is a number beyond the range of bf16 (overflow or underflow).
- Example: `bf16(0.5)` gives `0.5`

#### `f16`

```camel
f16: (x: i32) => f16
f16: (x: int) => f16
f16: (x: f32) => f16
f16: (x: float) => f16
f16: (x: f16) => f16
f16: (x: string) => f16
```

x as an f16: the nearest f16 of x, rounding to nearest with ties to even, once. The same
conversion as bf16, at the other reduced precision (design principles 7.3).

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidNumberText` when x is a string that is not a number; fault `ConversionOutOfRange` when x is a string that is a number beyond the range of f16 (overflow or underflow).
- Example: `f16(0.5)` gives `0.5`

#### `c64`

```camel
c64: (x: i32) => c64
c64: (x: int) => c64
c64: (x: f32) => c64
c64: (x: float) => c64
c64: (x: c64) => c64
c64: (x: c128) => c64
```

x as a 64-bit complex number: the real part is x and the imaginary part is zero. A c128
keeps both parts as they are.

- Pure.
- Example: `c64(2)` gives `2+0i`

#### `c128`

```camel
c128: (x: i32) => c128
c128: (x: int) => c128
c128: (x: f32) => c128
c128: (x: float) => c128
c128: (x: c64) => c128
c128: (x: c128) => c128
```

x as a 128-bit complex number: the real part is x and the imaginary part is zero.

- Pure.
- Example: `c128(2)` gives `2+0i`

#### `string`

```camel
string: (x: T) => string
```

x as text, as println writes it. A float is written as the shortest text that reads back as
the same number: string(2.5) is '2.5', string(2.0) is '2.0'.

- Pure.
- Example: `string(42)` gives `'42'`

#### `parse_int`

```camel
parse_int: (text: string) => int!
```

The integer a text spells, or an error value.

- Pure.
- Failure: error `ParseError` when the text is not, as a whole, one integer (blanks are not skipped).
- Example: `parse_int('42') !! 0` gives `42`

#### `parse_float`

```camel
parse_float: (text: string) => float!
```

The number a text spells, or an error value.

- Pure.
- Failure: error `ParseError` when the text is not a number.
- Example: `parse_float('2.5') !! 0.0` gives `2.5`

#### `error`

```camel
error: (kind: string, message: string) => Error
```

An Error value of the given kind with the given message; the compiler adds the source
position of the call. `throw error(...)` returns it from a function declared `T!`.

- Pure.
- Example: `throw error('RangeError', 'too large')`

### Input and output

#### `print`

```camel
print: (x: T, ...rest: U...) => T
```

Writes the arguments, separated by spaces, without a line end, and gives back the first one
(so that the write can be part of the data flow). The other arguments may each have a type
of their own. With a format, print<fmt>(...), writes the format with the arguments put in,
also without a line end.

- With effects: writes to standard output.
- Example: `print('a', 1)` gives `a 1`

#### `println`

```camel
println: (x: T, ...rest: U...) => T
```

Writes the arguments, separated by spaces, and a line end, and gives back the first one (so
that the write can be part of the data flow). The other arguments may each have a type of
their own. With a format, println<fmt>(...), writes the format with the arguments put in and
one line end.

- With effects: writes to standard output.
- Example: `println('a', 1)` gives `a 1`

#### `eprintln`

```camel
eprintln: (x: T, ...rest: U...) => T
```

Writes the arguments, separated by spaces, and a line end, to standard error, and gives back
the first one (so that the write can be part of the data flow). The other arguments may each
have a type of their own. With a format, eprintln<fmt>(...), writes the format with the
arguments put in and one line end.

- With effects: writes to standard error.
- Example: `eprintln('a', 1)` gives `a 1`

#### `input`

```camel
input: (prompt: string) => string
```

Writes prompt and reads one line from standard input.

- With effects: reads standard input.
- Example: `input('name: ')` gives `what the user typed`

#### `sleep`

```camel
sleep: (milliseconds: int) => void
```

Suspends the program for the given number of milliseconds.

- With effects: waits.
- Failure: fault `InvalidArgument` when the duration is negative.
- Example: `sleep(100)`

#### `exit`

```camel
exit: (code: int) => void
```

Ends the program with the given exit code, after writing buffered output.

- With effects: ends the program.
- Example: `exit(2)`

### Strings

#### `format`

```camel
format: <...args: T...> (fmt: string) => string
```

The text fmt with each `{}` placeholder replaced by the next argument; placeholders take
format specifications such as `{:.2f}` and `{:>8}`.

A specification whose argument is a numeric array acts on each element on its own, while the
brackets and the `, ` between the elements are the array's own form: `'{:.4f}'->format<xs>`
with `xs = [0.7692267, 0.780836, 0.77707076]` is `[0.7692, 0.7808, 0.7771]`, and an array of
rank 2 keeps one bracket level per dimension (`[[0.7692, 0.7808], [0.7771, 2.0000]]`). Each
element is written by the specification and by its own type, so `{:.2f}` rounds an `f32`
element and an `f64` element each at two places. An array without a specification prints as
it does everywhere else: every element in the shortest text that reads back as the same
number, which is `'{}'->format<xs>` giving `[0.7692267, 0.780836, 0.77707076]`.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `FormatFailed` when the placeholders and the arguments do not fit.
- Example: `'{} is {:.2f}'->format<'x', 2.5>` gives `'x is 2.50'`

#### `join`

```camel
join: <sep: string> (xs: string[]) => string
```

The strings of xs joined with sep between them.

- Pure.
- Example: `['a', 'b']->join<', '>` gives `'a, b'`

#### `len`

```camel
len: (x: string) => int
len: (x: T[..]) => int
```

The number of bytes of a string, or of the first dimension of an array of any rank.

- Pure.
- Example: `len('h€')` gives `4`

### Arrays

#### `range`

```camel
range: (start: int, end: int, step?: int) => int[]
```

The integers of a step: `start`, `start + step`, ... up to, not including, `end`; with no step
the step is 1, `range(a, b)` is the same sequence as the interval `a..b` and becomes it on the
graph (design principles 4.2). `step` must move: a step of 0 is a fault, and a constant call
with a step of 0 is refused where it is written. The result is empty when the step does not
carry `start` towards `end`. A `for` over an interval is fused by the compiler and builds no
array; this call builds one.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidArgument` when the step is 0.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `range(0, 10, 3)` gives `[0, 3, 6, 9]`
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `range(10, 0, -3)` gives `[10, 7, 4, 1]`
- Why it is not compiled: the interval is written `a..b`; the stepped form is `range(a, b, step)`

#### `head`

```camel
head: (xs: T[]) => T
```

The first element. An empty array has none: check len first.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `IndexOutOfRange` when the array is empty.
- Example: `head([1, 2, 3])` gives `1`

#### `last`

```camel
last: (xs: T[]) => T
```

The last element. An empty array has none: check len first. Negative indices are not
counted from the end (a negative index is a fault), so this is how the last element is
written.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `IndexOutOfRange` when the array is empty.
- Example: `last([1, 2, 3])` gives `3`

#### `tail`

```camel
tail: (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

The elements after the first; empty for an array of fewer than two elements.

- Pure.
- Example: `tail([1, 2, 3])` gives `[2, 3]`

#### `slice`

```camel
slice: <start: int, end: int> (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

The elements from index start up to, not including, end. Both are positions from 0 to the
length; a bound outside the array (a negative one included) is a fault, as an index out of
range is. `take` and `drop` of the module `array` cut to the array instead.

- Pure.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3, 4]->slice<1, 3>` gives `[2, 3]`

#### `slice`

```camel
slice: (t: T[], axis: int, start: int, end: int, step: int = 1, written: int = 3) => T[]
```

A slice of one axis of an array of values, written as a call: `slice(t, axis, a, b, s)` is the
same node the subscript `t[a:b:s]` builds -- the value, the axis, the two bounds, the step and
the mask saying which bounds were written. The function form writes both, so its mask is 3; any
axis and any rank are the core's; a negative or out-of-range bound is a fault, with the
subscript's one wording, and a step may be any non-zero value (the constant 0 is refused).
The last element is `last(t)` and an axis' length is `dim(t, axis)`, which is how a bound is
written where it used to count from the end.

- Pure.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3, 4]->slice(0, 1, 3)` gives `[2, 3]`

#### `slice`

```camel
slice: (s: string, axis: int, start: int, end: int, step: int = 1, written: int = 3) => string
```

The same slice of a string, by code point: a string has the one axis 0, and the result is a
string. `'中文字'[1:3]` and `slice('中文字', 0, 1, 3)` are both `'文字'`.

- Pure.
- Example: `slice('hello', 0, 1, 4)` gives `'ell'`

#### `slice`

```camel
slice: (b: Bytes, axis: int, start: int, end: int, step: int = 1, written: int = 3) => Bytes
```

The same slice of a `Bytes`, by byte: it has the one axis 0, and the result is a `Bytes`.
`b[1:3]` and `slice(b, 0, 1, 3)` are the same bytes.

- Pure.
- Example: `slice(encode('hello'), 0, 1, 4)` gives `the bytes of 'ell'`

#### `concat`

```camel
concat: (xs: T[], ys: T[]) => T[]
```

The elements of xs followed by those of ys, as a new array.

- Pure.
- Example: `concat([1], [2, 3])` gives `[1, 2, 3]`

#### `contains`

```camel
contains: <value: T> (xs: T[]) => bool
```

Whether an element of xs equals value, by the `==` of the element type (by content for
arrays, tuples and structs).

- Pure.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3]->contains<2>` gives `true`

#### `contains`

```camel
contains: <sub: string> (s: string) => bool
```

Whether sub occurs in the string s (bytes are compared). The empty string occurs in every
string.

- Pure.
- Example: `'hello'->contains<'ell'>` gives `true`

#### `zip`

```camel
zip: (xs: T[], ys: U[]) => (T, U)[]
```

Two arrays combined element by element into pairs. They must have the same length.
Three or more arrays (`zip(xs, ys, zs)`) give tuples of that many elements.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidArgument` when the lengths differ.
- Example: `zip([1, 2], ['a', 'b'])` gives `[(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')]`

#### `append`

```camel
append: <value: T> (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

A new array: the elements of xs, then value. xs is unchanged; to add to a variable, bind it
to the result: `acc = acc->append<4>` (as a statement, that form grows the array in place
when nothing else refers to it, which cannot be observed).

- Pure.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3]->append<4>` gives `[1, 2, 3, 4]`

#### `extend`

```camel
extend: <other: T[]> (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

A new array: the elements of xs, then those of other. xs is unchanged.

- Pure.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3]->extend<[4, 5]>` gives `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`

### Higher-order functions

`map` and `filter` apply f to the elements with no order among the calls: the parallel
scheduler may run them at the same time, and the result is by position. `foreach` and
`reduce` call f element by element in order. `T[]` is an array of that element type (rank 1); the rank-n meaning is P5
work. They are declared with effects because what a
call does is what f does.

#### `map`

```camel
map: <f: (item: T) => U> (xs: T[]) => U[]
```

f applied to every element; the calls have no order among them.

- With effects: what f does.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3]->map<(x: int) => x * 2>` gives `[2, 4, 6]`

#### `filter`

```camel
filter: <f: (item: T) => bool> (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

The elements for which f is true, in order; the calls of f have no order among them.

- With effects: what f does.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3, 4]->filter<(x: int) => x % 2 == 0>` gives `[2, 4]`

#### `reduce`

```camel
reduce: <f: (acc: U, item: T) => U, initial: U> (xs: T[]) => U
```

The elements combined from left to right: f(...f(f(initial, xs[0]), xs[1])..., xs[n-1]).

- With effects: what f does.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3]->reduce<(acc: int, x: int) => acc + x, 0>` gives `6`

#### `foreach`

```camel
foreach: <f: (item: T) => void> (xs: T[]) => void
```

Calls f for every element, in order.

- With effects: what f does.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3]->foreach<(x: int) => println(x)>`

#### `apply`

```camel
apply: <f: (item: T) => T> (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

A new array: f of every element of xs, which is unchanged; `map` where f keeps the element
type. The calls have no order among them, as for `map`.

- With effects: what f does.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3]->apply<(x: int) => x * 2>` gives `[2, 4, 6]`

### Fault isolation

A fault (a division by zero, an index out of range, a recursion that is too deep, ...) ends
the program with a located diagnostic. `attempt` isolates it at the boundary of one call
(design principles 3.9; docs/technical/33_fault_isolation.md). The name is provisional.

#### `attempt`

```camel
attempt: (f: (...args: A) => T, ...args: A) => T!
```

Calls f with the arguments. A fault raised inside the call becomes an error value whose kind
is the name of the fault (`DivisionByZero`, ...), with the fault's message and position;
otherwise the result of f. When f itself returns `U!`, so does attempt. What the call did
before the fault is not undone; exit() and the failures of the compiler itself are not
isolated.

- With effects: what f does.
- Example: `attempt((x: int) => 10 / x, 0) !! -1` gives `-1: the division fault becomes an error value`
- Example: `attempt((x: int) => 10 / x, 2) !! -1` gives `5`

#### `len`

```camel
len: (x: Map<K, V>) => int
len: (x: Set<T>) => int
```

The number of entries of a map or of elements of a set. The collection is `x`, the name the
string and array declarations above give their one parameter: the position means the value
whose length is asked for, whatever its type.

- Pure.
- Example: `len([('a', 1), ('b', 2)] as Map<string, int>)` gives `2`

#### `get`

```camel
get: <key: K> (m: Map<K, V>) => V?
```

The value stored under key, or null when the map has no such key. `m[key]` is the same lookup.

- Pure.
- Example: `([('a', 1)] as Map<string, int>)->get<'z'> ?? 0` gives `0 when the map has no 'z'`

#### `get_or`

```camel
get_or: <key: K, fallback: V> (m: Map<K, V>) => V
```

The value stored under key, or fallback when the map has no such key.

- Pure.
- Example: `([('a', 1)] as Map<string, int>)->get_or<'z', -1>` gives `-1 when the map has no 'z'`

#### `put`

```camel
put: <key: K, value: V> (m: Map<K, V>) => Map<K, V>
```

A map with value stored under key; an existing entry of that key is replaced. m is unchanged.

- Pure.
- Example: `([('a', 1), ('b', 2)] as Map<string, int>)->put<'c', 3>` gives `{a: 1, b: 2, c: 3}`

#### `remove`

```camel
remove: <key: K> (c: Map<K, V>) => Map<K, V>
remove: (c: Set<K>) => Set<K>
```

A map without the entry of key, or a set without the element; a key or element that is not there changes nothing. The argument is unchanged.

- Pure.
- Example: `([('a', 1), ('b', 2)] as Map<string, int>)->remove<'a'>` gives `{b: 2}`

#### `has`

```camel
has: <key: K> (c: Map<K, V>) => bool
has: (c: Set<K>) => bool
```

Whether a map has an entry of key, or a set has the element.

- Pure.
- Example: `([('a', 1)] as Map<string, int>)->has<'a'>` gives `true`

#### `keys`

```camel
keys: (m: Map<K, V>) => K[]
```

The keys of a map, in ascending order.

- Pure.
- Example: `keys([('b', 2), ('a', 1)] as Map<string, int>)` gives `[a, b]`

#### `values`

```camel
values: (m: Map<K, V>) => V[]
```

The values of a map, in the ascending order of their keys.

- Pure.
- Example: `values([('b', 2), ('a', 1)] as Map<string, int>)` gives `[1, 2]`

#### `items`

```camel
items: (m: Map<K, V>) => (K, V)[]
```

The entries of a map as (key, value) tuples, in ascending order of the keys.

- Pure.
- Example: `items([('b', 2), ('a', 1)] as Map<string, int>)` gives `[(a, 1), (b, 2)]`

#### `items`

```camel
items: (m: Set<T>) => T[]
```

The elements of a set as an array, in ascending order. The collection is `m`, the name the
map declaration above gives its one parameter: the position means the collection whose items
are listed.

- Pure.
- Example: `items([3, 1, 2] as Set<int>)` gives `[1, 2, 3]`

#### `merge`

```camel
merge: (m: Map<K, V>, other: Map<K, V>) => Map<K, V>
```

A map with the entries of both maps; for a key in both, the entry of other is taken. Neither argument is changed.

- Pure.
- Example: `merge([('a', 1), ('b', 2)] as Map<string, int>, [('b', 20), ('c', 30)] as Map<string, int>)` gives `{a: 1, b: 20, c: 30}`

#### `contains`

```camel
contains: <value: T> (s: Set<T>) => bool
```

Whether value is an element of the set.

- Pure.
- Example: `([1, 2, 3] as Set<int>)->contains<9>` gives `false`

#### `add`

```camel
add: <value: T> (s: Set<T>) => Set<T>
```

A set with value added; s is unchanged.

- Pure.
- Example: `([1, 2, 3] as Set<int>)->add<9>` gives `{1, 2, 3, 9}`

#### `union`

```camel
union: (s: Set<T>, other: Set<T>) => Set<T>
```

The set of the elements that are in either set.

- Pure.
- Example: `union([1, 2, 3] as Set<int>, [3, 4] as Set<int>)` gives `{1, 2, 3, 4}`

#### `intersect`

```camel
intersect: (s: Set<T>, other: Set<T>) => Set<T>
```

The set of the elements that are in both sets.

- Pure.
- Example: `intersect([1, 2, 3] as Set<int>, [3, 4] as Set<int>)` gives `{3}`

#### `difference`

```camel
difference: (s: Set<T>, other: Set<T>) => Set<T>
```

The set of the elements of s that are not in other.

- Pure.
- Example: `difference([1, 2, 3] as Set<int>, [3, 4] as Set<int>)` gives `{1, 2}`

#### `is_subset`

```camel
is_subset: (s: Set<T>, other: Set<T>) => bool
```

Whether every element of s is an element of other.

- Pure.
- Example: `is_subset([1, 2] as Set<int>, [1, 2, 3] as Set<int>)` gives `true`

### Streams

#### `tee_note`

```camel
tee_note: (hint: int, cap: int, elements: int, peak: int, s: T..) => void
```

Records one `tee` (design principles 5.4) for the report of a profile session: the hint it
took, the widest hint the implementation honours, the elements it has pulled from its source so
far, and the most elements it has buffered at once -- with the stream it reads, whose value
tells one tee from another and whose type the operator takes, and whose elements it does not.
A program does not write this: `tee` calls it once per element it pulls, and `std::profile`
prints what it recorded (`STREAM_TEE`).

- With effects: records the numbers of the tee.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `tee_note(8, 64, 2, 2, s)` gives `the tee written `tee(s, 8)` reports itself this way`
- Why it is not compiled: the last operand is the stream a tee reads, and no example program has one

<a id="str"></a>

## `str`: strings

Text functions. A string is always valid UTF-8, and its length and indices count code points:
`len('中文')` is 2 and `'中文'[0]` is `'中'`. Binary data is `Bytes`; `bytes::encode` and
`bytes::decode` are the one place where a string becomes UTF-8 bytes and back.

- The string a function works on is its ordinary argument; everything that configures the
  call is a with-argument, so calls chain: `s->trim->split<','>`.
- Every function returns a new string; none changes its argument.
- A result that may not exist is `T?` (`index_of`, `strip_prefix`). A number that is not a
  code point is an error value (`from_codepoints`). An index outside the string is a fault.
- Only what Camel cannot say about a string is native: code points as numbers and
  letter case (cutting by code point is the subscript `s[a:b]` of the core). The rest is
  written here; `index_of` and `split` carry a native kernel under `#impl` for speed, with the same result as their bodies.

### Native primitives

#### `codepoints`

```camel
codepoints: (s: string) => int[]
```

The code points of s, as numbers.

- Pure.
- Example: `codepoints('h€')` gives `[104, 8364]`

#### `from_codepoints`

```camel
from_codepoints: (xs: int[]) => string!
```

The string made of the given code points.

- Pure.
- Failure: error `EncodingError` when an element is not a code point (negative, above 0x10FFFF, or a surrogate).
- Example: `from_codepoints([104, 8364]) !! ''` gives `'h€'`

#### `to_upper`

```camel
to_upper: (s: string) => string
```

s with every letter in upper case, by the Unicode simple (one code point to one code point)
case mapping; a letter without one is kept as it is.

- Pure.
- Example: `to_upper('héllo')` gives `'HÉLLO'`

#### `to_lower`

```camel
to_lower: (s: string) => string
```

s with every letter in lower case, by the Unicode simple case mapping.

- Pure.
- Example: `to_lower('HeLLo')` gives `'hello'`

### Searching

#### `index_of`

```camel
index_of: <sub: string> (s: string) => int?
```

The index (in code points) of the first occurrence of sub in s, or null when there is none.
An empty sub is found at 0.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `'hello'->index_of<'l'>` gives `2`

#### `starts_with`

```camel
starts_with: <prefix: string> (s: string) => bool
```

Whether s begins with prefix. Every string begins with the empty string.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `'hello'->starts_with<'he'>` gives `true`

#### `ends_with`

```camel
ends_with: <suffix: string> (s: string) => bool
```

Whether s ends with suffix. Every string ends with the empty string.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `'hello'->ends_with<'lo'>` gives `true`

#### `strip_prefix`

```camel
strip_prefix: <prefix: string> (s: string) => string?
```

s without the prefix at its start, or null when s does not begin with it.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `'v1.2'->strip_prefix<'v'>` gives `'1.2'`

#### `strip_suffix`

```camel
strip_suffix: <suffix: string> (s: string) => string?
```

s without the suffix at its end, or null when s does not end with it.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `'a.cml'->strip_suffix<'.cml'>` gives `'a'`

### Cutting and joining

#### `split`

```camel
split: <sep: string> (s: string) => string[]
```

The pieces of s between occurrences of sep. An empty s gives one empty piece; a separator at
the start or the end gives an empty piece there. An empty sep cuts s into its code points
(no pieces for an empty s).

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `'a,b,,c'->split<','>` gives `['a', 'b', '', 'c']`

#### `lines`

```camel
lines: (s: string) => string[]
```

The lines of s, cut at a line feed or a carriage return followed by a line feed. A line
feed at the very end does not start another line.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `'a\r\nb\n'->lines` gives `['a', 'b']`

#### `replace`

```camel
replace: <old: string, new: string> (s: string) => string
```

s with every occurrence of old replaced by new, found from left to right without overlap.
An empty old puts new between the code points of s.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `'a-b-c'->replace<'-', '+'>` gives `'a+b+c'`

#### `repeat`

```camel
repeat: <count: int> (s: string) => string
```

s written count times in a row; the empty string when count is not positive.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `'ab'->repeat<3>` gives `'ababab'`

### White space

#### `trim_start`

```camel
trim_start: (s: string) => string
```

s without the ASCII white space (space, tab, line feed, carriage return, vertical tab, form
feed) at its start.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `trim_start('  hi  ')` gives `'hi  '`

#### `trim_end`

```camel
trim_end: (s: string) => string
```

s without the ASCII white space at its end.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `trim_end('  hi  ')` gives `'  hi'`

#### `trim`

```camel
trim: (s: string) => string
```

s without the ASCII white space at both ends. Other white space, such as U+00A0, is kept.

- With effects: not pure.
- Example: `trim('  hi \n')` gives `'hi'`

<a id="bytes"></a>

## `bytes`: immutable binary values and UTF-8 conversion

Binary data. `Bytes` is an immutable value of the core; a string is text and never holds
arbitrary bytes, so the only crossing between the two is `encode` and `decode`.

Length (`len`), concatenation (`a + b`) and cutting (`b[a:b]`) are the core's, as they are for
a string. What is here converts, and is native: a `Bytes` is a data block, and reading or
building one needs the layout control the language does not show (design principles 10.4).

#### `encode`

```camel
encode: (text: string) => Bytes
```

The UTF-8 bytes of text.

- Pure.
- Example: `encode('hello')`

#### `decode`

```camel
decode: (content: Bytes) => string!
```

The text the bytes spell. Bytes that are not valid UTF-8 are an error value, not a fault: they
come from the outside world.

- Pure.
- Failure: error `EncodingError` when the bytes are not valid UTF-8 or the text is larger than a string can be.
- Example: `decode(encode('中文')) !! ''` gives `'中文'`

#### `from_array`

```camel
from_array: (values: int[]) => Bytes
```

The bytes with the given values.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `InvalidArgument` when an element is outside 0..255.
- Example: `from_array([0, 128, 255])`

#### `to_array`

```camel
to_array: (content: Bytes) => int[]
```

The values of the bytes, each in 0..255.

- Pure.
- Example: `to_array(encode('AB'))` gives `[65, 66]`

<a id="ckpt"></a>

## `ckpt`: parameter trees and checkpoints

#### `tree_leaves`

```camel
tree_leaves: (tree: T) => L
```

The leaves of a tree, as a tuple.

- Pure.
- Example: `tree_leaves({ a: 1, b: (2, 3) })` gives `(1, 2, 3)`

#### `save_tree`

```camel
save_tree: (dir: string, tree: T, dataset_manifest_sha256?: string) => void
```

Saves a tree to a directory, one file per leaf named by its path (`blocks.0.w.npy` for a
tensor), with a manifest that records the types, sizes and SHA-256 sums and, when
`dataset_manifest_sha256` is given, that hash of the data manifest. The directory is
replaced as a whole or not at all: the new checkpoint is written and flushed into a
temporary sibling and renamed into place, and the old directory is kept beside it as the
hidden sibling `.<name>.ckpt-previous` (the destination's own directory name between a
leading dot and `.ckpt-previous`) until that rename succeeds, so a failure puts the old
directory back. A destination that does not exist is created; one that does is replaced; a
symbolic link or a reparse point there is refused. If the process dies between the two
renames, `load_tree` reads `.<name>.ckpt-previous` and the next `save_tree` restores it
before replacing it. (A directory rename cannot replace a non-empty directory on Windows or
POSIX, hence the two renames.) A leaf type a checkpoint cannot hold (anything but a tensor,
`Bytes`, `string`, `bool`, `i32`, `int`, `f32`, `f64`) is a compile-time error that names
the path. Only one writer may save to a directory at a time: concurrent `save_tree` calls
for the same directory are not serialized (there is no lock file), so the contract is a
single writer; one of two racing saves fails explicitly, and a reader still sees a complete
checkpoint.

- With effects: writes and replaces the directory.
- Failure: fault `FileSystemError` when the directory cannot be written or published.
- Example: `save_tree('out/ckpt', { w: 1.0, step: 10 })`

#### `load_tree`

```camel
load_tree: (dir: string, dataset_manifest_sha256?: string) => T!
```

Reads a tree of the type T back from a directory `save_tree` wrote, checking the structure,
the types, the sizes and the SHA-256 sums first: a directory that does not fit T is a
`CheckpointError` value, nothing is partly loaded. A `dataset_manifest_sha256` that differs
from the one the checkpoint records is a warning on standard error, not an error. T is the
explicit type argument or the
expected type of the result. When a save was interrupted after moving the old directory
aside, the complete `.<name>.ckpt-previous` sibling is read instead, with a warning on
standard error; the next save restores it before replacing it.

- With effects: reads the directory.
- Failure: error value `CheckpointError` when the directory does not hold a tree of the type T, or a file is missing or does not match its recorded sum.
- Example: `load_tree::<{ w: float, step: int }>('out/ckpt') !! { w: 0.0, step: 0 }`

<a id="tree"></a>

## `tree`: parameter trees written in Camel

The parameter-tree library written in Camel (design principles 13.5): a tree is a value made
of nested structs and tuples, and everything else is a leaf.

`tree_paths`, `tree_map`, `tree_reduce` and `tree_unzip` are written here, with `match type`,
`static for`/`static loop`, `fields`, `indices`, `typeof` and rest parameters: the walk is
expanded at each call into ordinary access and fill nodes, with no function of its own per
leaf type. Each exported function recurses itself. `paths_at` and `unzip_at` stay because
they carry a value the exported signature does not have (the path built so far, the component
of the leaf tuple): a default argument would fold the first one into `tree_paths` (the
language has none yet), and the second is not a hand-off but the walk of one component.

`tree_leaves` is not here yet. The leaves are one flat tuple whose length is the sum of the
leaves of every field, and Camel cannot splice a tuple value's elements into a tuple being
built: `( ..ts )` is not written (a rest argument is only a call argument), and a function
with a rest parameter has no value to return. It stays `ckpt:tree_leaves` until value-tuple
expansion exists.

The path of a leaf is its field names (tuple indices) from the root, joined by dots; the
root's own path is the empty string. The path values are ordinary strings, so the result is
the same tree with a `string` at every leaf.

#### `tree_paths`

```camel
tree_paths: (t: T) => ?
```

The path of every leaf, as a tree of the same shape.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `tree_paths({ a: 1, b: (2, 3) })` gives `{ a: 'a', b: ('b.0', 'b.1') }`

#### `tree_map`

```camel
tree_map: <f: F> (t: T, ..ts) => ?
```

Applies f to the leaves in the same place of the trees (one tree, or several of the same
shape: the callback then takes one leaf of each), and gives a tree of the results. The shape
is that of the first tree.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `tree_map<(x: int): int => x + 1>({ a: 1, b: (2, 3) })` gives `{ a: 2, b: (3, 4) }`

#### `tree_reduce`

```camel
tree_reduce: <f: (acc: R, leaf: A) => R> (t: T, init: R) => R
```

Folds the leaves from the first to the last with f, starting from init.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `tree_reduce<(acc: int, x: int): int => acc + x>({ a: 1, b: (2, 3) }, 0)` gives `6`

#### `tree_unzip`

```camel
tree_unzip: (r: R, s: S) => ?
```

Turns a tree of tuples into a tuple of trees: the shape is that of `reference`, and every
leaf of `tree` at a leaf of the reference is a tuple of the same length.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `tree_unzip({ a: (1, 2.0) }, { a: 0 })` gives `({ a: 1 }, { a: 2.0 })`

<a id="tensor"></a>

## `tensor`: multi-dimensional numeric arrays

The `tensor` module: multi-dimensional numeric arrays, their element type and extents, their
binary form, a NumPy file, and the module's worker threads and random generator.

The declarations written here are the operators whose signature is fixed. The ones whose element
type or shape follows their arguments — elementwise arithmetic, the reshaping operators, the
axis forms of a reduction — cannot be written as a declaration; they are implemented in
`modules/tensor` and listed in `stdlib/signatures/tensor.cml`, whose entries this page renders
under the same sections (design principles 6.4).

### Creation

#### `new`

```camel
new: (values: float[..] | number[]) => float[..]
```

A tensor made of a nested number array (or of a tensor, copied into contiguous row-major
storage); the element type follows the values: `float` for a float (design principles 5.1: a
float literal's own type is `float`, which is `f64`), `int64` for an integer and `bool` for a
boolean.

- Pure.
- Example: `new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])`

#### `empty`

```camel
empty: (shape: int[]) => f32[..]
```

A tensor of the given extents; the allocation is zeroed, so it reads as `zeros` of the same
shape.

- Pure.
- Example: `empty([2, 3])`

#### `zeros`

```camel
zeros: (shape: int[]) => f32[..]
```

A tensor of `f32` zeros with the given extents.

- Pure.
- Example: `zeros([2, 3])`

#### `ones`

```camel
ones: (shape: int[]) => f32[..]
```

A tensor of `f32` ones with the given extents.

- Pure.
- Example: `ones([2, 3])`

#### `full`

```camel
full: (shape: int[], value: number) => float[..]
```

A tensor of the given extents whose elements are all value; the element type is the value's.

- Pure.
- Example: `full([2, 2], -1.0)`

#### `eye`

```camel
eye: (n: int) => f32[..]
```

The `f32` n by n identity matrix.

- Pure.
- Example: `eye(2)`

#### `range`

```camel
range: (start: int, stop?: int, step?: int) => int64[..]
```

The integer sequence start, start + step, ... below stop, as a rank-1 `int64` tensor: one
argument is stop with start 0, step is 1 by default, and a step of 0 is a fault.

The interval of the language's own integers is written `a..b` (design principles 4.2), so a
two-argument `range(a, b)` written without a module qualifier is the language's built-in
interval and is refused: the two-parameter `range` is gone. This function is reached for one
argument, for three, or by the qualified name `tensor::range(...)`.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when stop and start leave a step of 0.
- Example: `range(0, 10, 2)` gives `[0, 2, 4, 6, 8]`

### Random

#### `random`

```camel
random: (shape: int[], low: number, high: number) => f32[..]
```

A tensor of `f32` values drawn uniformly from [low, high) with the given extents.

- With effects: reads and advances the random generator.
- Example: `random([2, 2], 0.0, 1.0)`

#### `randn`

```camel
randn: (shape: int[], mean?: number, std?: number) => f32[..]
```

A tensor of `f32` values drawn from the normal distribution with the given mean (0 by
default) and standard deviation (1 by default), with the given extents.

- With effects: reads and advances the random generator.
- Example: `randn([2, 3])`

### Elementwise

#### `add`

```camel
add: (lhs: float[..] | number, rhs: float[..] | number) => float[..]
```

a + b per element, with NumPy broadcasting: a scalar operand applies to every element, and
the element type is the wider of the two (a float with an integer gives `f32`).

- Pure.
- Example: `add(new([1.0, 2.0]), 1.0)` gives `[2.0, 3.0]`

#### `subtract`

```camel
subtract: (lhs: float[..] | number, rhs: float[..] | number) => float[..]
```

a - b per element, with NumPy broadcasting.

- Pure.
- Example: `subtract(new([1.0, 2.0]), 0.5)` gives `[0.5, 1.5]`

#### `multiply`

```camel
multiply: (lhs: float[..] | number, rhs: float[..] | number) => float[..]
```

a * b per element, with NumPy broadcasting.

- Pure.
- Example: `multiply(new([1.0, 2.0]), new([3.0, 4.0]))` gives `[3.0, 8.0]`

#### `divide`

```camel
divide: (lhs: float[..] | number, rhs: float[..] | number) => float[..]
```

a / b per element, with NumPy broadcasting; IEEE division: x / 0 is an infinity or NaN, not a
fault.

- Pure.
- Example: `divide(new([1.0, 2.0]), 2.0)` gives `[0.5, 1.0]`

#### `pow`

```camel
pow: (lhs: float[..] | number, rhs: float[..] | number) => float[..]
```

a raised to b per element, with NumPy broadcasting.

- Pure.
- Example: `pow(new([2.0, 3.0]), 2.0)` gives `[4.0, 9.0]`

#### `maximum`

```camel
maximum: (lhs: float[..] | number, rhs: float[..] | number) => float[..]
```

IEEE 754-2019 maximum per element, with NumPy broadcasting: NaN on either side gives the
canonical quiet NaN, and -0 is below +0.

- Pure.
- Example: `maximum(new([1.0, -0.0]), 0.0)` gives `[1.0, 0.0]`

#### `minimum`

```camel
minimum: (lhs: float[..] | number, rhs: float[..] | number) => float[..]
```

IEEE 754-2019 minimum per element, with NumPy broadcasting: NaN on either side gives the
canonical quiet NaN, and -0 is below +0.

- Pure.
- Example: `minimum(new([1.0, -0.0]), 0.0)` gives `[0.0, -0.0]`

#### `mod`

```camel
mod: (lhs: float[..] | number, rhs: float[..] | number) => float[..]
```

a % b per element, with NumPy broadcasting: the language's remainder, the truncated one
(`camel::utils::remainder`), so the result takes the sign of the left operand and nothing is
floored — a negative a and a positive b give a negative result. On a floating element type it
is `fmod`, in the element type's own precision: a bf16 or f16 array computes in f32 and rounds
once when it is stored. A divisor of zero gives NaN for a floating element type, as IEEE
division does; an integer element type has the integer remainder.

- Pure.
- Example: `mod(new([7.5, -7.5]), 2.0)` gives `[1.5, -1.5]`

#### `where`

```camel
where: (cond: bool[..], lhs: float[..] | number, rhs: float[..] | number) => float[..]
```

lhs where cond holds, rhs elsewhere, broadcast to one shape; the element type is the wider of
lhs and rhs.

- Pure.
- Example: `where(new([true, false]), new([1.0, 2.0]), 0.0)` gives `[1.0, 0.0]`

#### `neg`

```camel
neg: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

-x per element: the sign flipped.

- Pure.
- Example: `neg(new([1.0, -2.0]))` gives `[-1.0, 2.0]`

#### `abs`

```camel
abs: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

|x| per element: the sign cleared.

- Pure.
- Example: `abs(new([-1.5, 2.0]))` gives `[1.5, 2.0]`

#### `exp`

```camel
exp: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

e^x per element, within 2 ulp, subnormal results included.

- Pure.
- Example: `exp(new([0.0, 1.0]))` gives `[1.0, 2.7182817]`

#### `log`

```camel
log: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

ln x per element, within 2 ulp; NaN, +-inf, +-0 and negative x are exact (negative x gives
NaN).

- Pure.
- Example: `log(new([1.0, 2.7182817]))` gives `[0.0, 1.0]`

#### `sqrt`

```camel
sqrt: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

sqrt(x) per element, rounded once in `f32`.

- Pure.
- Example: `sqrt(new([4.0, 9.0]))` gives `[2.0, 3.0]`

#### `rsqrt`

```camel
rsqrt: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

1 / sqrt(x) per element: two steps, each rounded in `f32`.

- Pure.
- Example: `rsqrt(new([4.0]))` gives `[0.5]`

#### `sigmoid`

```camel
sigmoid: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

The logistic function 1 / (1 + e^-x) per element.

- Pure.
- Example: `sigmoid(new([0.0]))` gives `[0.5]`

#### `tanh`

```camel
tanh: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

The hyperbolic tangent per element.

- Pure.
- Example: `tanh(new([0.0]))` gives `[0.0]`

#### `relu`

```camel
relu: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

maximum(x, +0) per element: NaN gives the canonical NaN, and -0 gives +0.

- Pure.
- Example: `relu(new([-1.0, 2.0]))` gives `[0.0, 2.0]`

#### `gelu`

```camel
gelu: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

The Gaussian error linear unit per element, computed as its normative definition in Camel.

- Pure.
- Example: `gelu(new([0.0]))` gives `[0.0]`

#### `erf`

```camel
erf: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

The Gauss error function per element.

- Pure.
- Example: `erf(new([0.0]))` gives `[0.0]`

### Shape and reshaping

#### `reshape`

```camel
reshape: (t: float[..] | number[], shape: int[]) => float[..]
```

The elements in row-major order, in a new shape; one extent may be -1, which the element
count fills.

- Pure.
- Example: `reshape(new([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]), [2, 2])`

#### `flatten`

```camel
flatten: (t: float[..], axis?: int) => float[..]
```

The elements in row-major order in two axes: the extents before axis multiplied into the
first, the rest into the second (axis 1 by default).

- Pure.
- Example: `flatten(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]))`

#### `unsqueeze`

```camel
unsqueeze: (t: float[..], axis: int) => float[..]
```

The elements unchanged, with an axis of extent 1 added at axis.

- Pure.
- Example: `unsqueeze(new([1.0, 2.0]), 0)` gives `shape [1, 2]`

#### `transpose`

```camel
transpose: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

The last two axes swapped (a vector becomes a column, a matrix its transpose).

- Pure.
- Example: `transpose(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]))`

#### `permute`

```camel
permute: (t: float[..], perm: int[]) => float[..]
```

The axes reordered as perm lists them.

- Pure.
- Example: `permute(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]), [1, 0])`

#### `concat`

```camel
concat: (a: float[..] | number[], b: float[..] | number[], axis: int) => float[..]
```

a and b joined along axis; every other extent must agree.

- Pure.
- Example: `concat(new([[1.0]]), new([[2.0]]), 0)` gives `shape [2, 1]`

#### `take`

```camel
take: (t: float[..], indices: int64[..] | number[]) => float[..]
```

The entries of the first axis that indices name, in that order.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when an index is outside the first axis.
- Example: `take(new([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]]), [2, 0])` gives `[[3.0], [1.0]]`

#### `one_hot`

```camel
one_hot: (labels: int64[..] | number[], classes: int) => int64[..]
```

Each label (an integer below classes) expanded to a row of classes with a 1 at its position:
an `int64` tensor of shape [labels, classes].

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `IndexOutOfRange` when a label is outside [0, classes), and fault `InvalidArgument` when classes is negative.
- Example: `one_hot(new([0, 2]), 3)` gives `[[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1]]`

#### `shape`

```camel
shape: (t: T[..]) => int[] when is_numeric::<T>()
```

The extents of a tensor, in order.

- Pure.
- Example: `shape(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]))` gives `[2, 2]`

#### `numel`

```camel
numel: (t: T[..]) => int when is_numeric::<T>()
```

The number of elements in a tensor: the product of its extents.

- Pure.
- Example: `numel(zeros([2, 3]))` gives `6`

#### `dim`

```camel
dim: (t: T[..], axis: int) => int when is_numeric::<T>()
dim: (t: T[..], axis: i32) => int when is_numeric::<T>()
```

The extent of one axis; a negative axis counts from the last one (`-1` is the last axis).

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is outside the rank.
- Example: `dim(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]), 1)` gives `2`

### Reduction

#### `sum`

```camel
sum: (t: T[..]) => T
```

The sum of every element, in the operand's element type: the canonical form of the element
type `T` is `sum::<T>(x: T[..]): T = T(sum(float(x)))`, so the elements are widened into an
`f64` accumulator (`float(x)`), the additions happen in `f64` in row-major order from +0, and
their sum is rounded into `T` once, at the end — the same element type and the same one
rounding as the axis form below, so the full form and the axis form agree bit for bit
(design principles 7.3). An `int64`, `int32` or `bool` tensor has no float accumulator: it is
summed exactly in `int64`, wrapping on overflow as integer arithmetic does (design principles
5.1, 7.7), and that exact value is the answer — `int64` as it stands, `int32` truncated into
its element type, `bool` as `int64`.

- Pure.
- Example: `sum(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]))` gives `10.0`

#### `sum`

```camel
sum: (t: float[..], axis: int, keepdims?: bool) => float[..]
```

The same sum over one axis, in an `f64` accumulator; keepdims keeps the axis with extent 1.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is outside the rank.
- Example: `sum(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]), 0)` gives `[4.0, 6.0]`

#### `mean`

```camel
mean: (t: T[..]) => T
```

The mean of every element, in the operand's element type, with one rounding: the canonical
form of the element type `T` is `mean::<T>(x: T[..]): T = T(sum(float(x)) / float(numel(x)))`.
The sum and the division by the element count both happen in `f64`, and their result is
rounded into `T` once — never a sum rounded to the element type and divided again, which
would round twice. A mean of an integer or bool tensor is `f32`, as by axis; an empty tensor
is a fault.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `DivisionByZero` when the tensor has no element.
- Example: `mean(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]))` gives `2.5`

#### `mean`

```camel
mean: (t: float[..], axis: int, keepdims?: bool) => float[..]
```

The same mean over one axis; keepdims keeps the axis with extent 1.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is outside the rank, and fault `DivisionByZero` when the axis is empty.
- Example: `mean(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]), 1)` gives `[1.5, 3.5]`

#### `max`

```camel
max: (t: float[..], axis: int, keepdims?: bool) => float[..]
```

IEEE 754-2019 maximum over the axis (exactly associative and commutative: any order gives
the same bits); keepdims keeps the axis with extent 1.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is outside the rank, and fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is empty.
- Example: `max(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]), 0)` gives `[3.0, 4.0]`

#### `min`

```camel
min: (t: float[..], axis: int, keepdims?: bool) => float[..]
```

IEEE 754-2019 minimum over the axis (exactly associative and commutative); keepdims keeps the
axis with extent 1.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is outside the rank, and fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is empty.
- Example: `min(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]), 1)` gives `[1.0, 3.0]`

#### `argmax`

```camel
argmax: (t: float[..], axis: int, keepdims?: bool) => int64[..]
```

The position (`int64`) of the first maximum over the axis by IEEE 754-2019 maximum: the first
NaN if there is one, +0 above -0, the earlier position on a tie.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is outside the rank, and fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is empty.
- Example: `argmax(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]), 1)` gives `[1, 1]`

#### `argmin`

```camel
argmin: (t: float[..], axis: int, keepdims?: bool) => int64[..]
```

The position (`int64`) of the first minimum over the axis by IEEE 754-2019 minimum: the first
NaN if there is one, -0 below +0, the earlier position on a tie.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is outside the rank, and fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is empty.
- Example: `argmin(new([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]), 0)` gives `[0, 0]`

#### `softmax`

```camel
softmax: (t: f32[..], axis?: int) => f32[..]
```

The softmax over the axis (-1, the last axis, by default), computed as its normative
definition in Camel, in `f32`.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is outside the rank.
- Example: `softmax(new([[1.0, 1.0]]))` gives `[[0.5, 0.5]]`

#### `log_softmax`

```camel
log_softmax: (t: f32[..], axis?: int) => f32[..]
```

The log of the softmax over the axis (-1 by default), computed as its normative definition in
Camel, in `f32`.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is outside the rank.
- Example: `log_softmax(new([[1.0, 1.0]]))` gives `[[-0.6931472, -0.6931472]]`

#### `softmax_grad`

```camel
softmax_grad: (y: f32[..], dy: f32[..], axis?: int) => f32[..]
```

The gradient of the softmax of y with the incoming gradient dy, over the axis (-1 by default).

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the axis is outside the rank.
- Example: `softmax_grad(y, dy)`

#### `layer_norm`

```camel
layer_norm: (x: f32[..], gamma: f32[..], beta: f32[..], eps?: number) => f32[..]
```

Layer normalization of x with gamma and beta, whose extents are the trailing ones of x, over
the trailing axes; eps is 1e-5 by default. The result is `f32`.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `TensorDimensionMismatch` when gamma or beta does not match the trailing extents of x.
- Example: `layer_norm(x, gamma, beta)`

### Linear algebra

#### `matmul`

```camel
matmul: (lhs: float[..], rhs: float[..]) => float[..]
```

The matrix product of lhs and rhs: per output element acc = +0, then acc = fma(a[i][k],
b[k][j], acc) for k ascending, every fused multiply-add rounded once in `f32`.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `TensorDimensionMismatch` when the inner extents do not agree.
- Example: `matmul(new([[1.0, 2.0]]), new([[3.0], [4.0]]))` gives `[[11.0]]`

#### `linear`

```camel
linear: (x: f32[..], weight: f32[..], bias?: f32[..]) => f32[..]
```

The affine transform of x by a rank-2 weight [in, out] whose rows are the features of x, plus
a rank-1 bias [out] when given.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `TensorDimensionMismatch` when the features of x are not the rows of weight, or bias is not rank 1 of the output extent.
- Example: `linear(x, weight, bias)`

### Gradient

#### `zeros_like`

```camel
zeros_like: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

A tensor of zeros shaped and typed like t.

- Pure.
- Example: `zeros_like(new([[1.0, 2.0]]))`

#### `ones_like`

```camel
ones_like: (t: float[..]) => float[..]
```

A tensor of ones shaped and typed like t.

- Pure.
- Example: `ones_like(new([[1.0, 2.0]]))`

### Conversion and display

#### `cast`

```camel
cast: (t: float[..] | number[], dtype: string) => int64[..]
```

t converted to the element type the name gives: "float32", "float", "double" or "float64"
for `f32`; "bfloat16" or "bf16" for `bf16`; "float16", "half" or "f16" for `f16`; "int64",
"int", "long" or "int32" for `int64`; "bool" for `bool`. The extents do not change.

A conversion into `bf16` or `f16` rounds (to nearest, ties to even). Writing the conversion
asks for that precision, so it needs no numeric permission: `change_precision` governs a
computation the compiler moves to lower precision (design principles 7.2-7.3). Reading a
`bf16` or `f16` tensor into a wider type is exact for every stored value.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the name is not one of those.
- Example: `cast(new([1.0, 2.0]), 'int64')` gives `[1, 2]`

#### `load_npy`

```camel
load_npy: (path: string) => T[..]
```

The tensor a NumPy `.npy` file holds, as the element type the program declares: the extents are
the file's (read them with `shape`, or check them with `as`), and the file's element type must
be `T` -- a file of another element type is a fault, never a conversion (design principles 5.1,
5.5). `T` is `f32`, `f64`, `i32`, `i64` or `bool`, the element types the format's storage types
(`'<f4'`, `'<f8'`, `'<i4'`, `'<i8'`, `'|b1'`) map to, exactly the type given. It is written at
the call (`load_npy::<f32>(p)`) or taken from the type of the position the call stands in
(`f32[3]`, `f32[..]`); `T` is the one type variable no parameter mentions, so a call
that says neither is not a use of this operator.

- With effects: reads a file.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the file is missing, is not a NumPy file, holds a storage type the module does not read, or holds another element type than `T`.
- Example: `load_npy::<f32>('x.npy')`

#### `show`

```camel
show: (t: A[..]) => void
```

Prints t to the console, in the module's layout.

- With effects: writes the console.
- Example: `show(new([[1.0, 2.0]]))`

### Binary form

#### `from_bytes`

```camel
from_bytes: (bytes: Bytes, shape: int[]) => T[..] when is_plain::<T>()
```

An array of the given shape made of little-endian elements: the payload `to_bytes` wrote. The
element type is the explicit type argument (`from_bytes::<f32>(b, [2])`) or comes from the
expected type of the result; it is `f32`, `f64`, `bf16`, `f16`, `i32`, `i64` or `bool`, exactly
the type given, or a struct or tuple whose fields are all pure data, which takes its element
type from the call (`from_bytes::<P>(b, [2])`) -- a declaration's parameters cannot mention a
type variable that only the result mentions. The element's bytes are its layout's, written as
`to_bytes` wrote them. A byte count that does not fit the shape is a fault. The bits are
copied: reading `bf16` or `f16` here passes the stored values through without rounding, so it
needs no numeric permission.

- Pure.
- Failure: fault `TensorDimensionMismatch` when the number of bytes does not fit the shape and the element type.
- Example: `from_bytes::<f32>(to_bytes(new([1.0, 2.0])), [2])`

#### `to_bytes`

```camel
to_bytes: (t: T[..]) => Bytes when is_plain::<T>()
```

The elements of a tensor as little-endian bytes, in row-major order: the payload `from_bytes`
reads back. The elements are the tensor's own bytes, so every pure-data element type has them:
one byte an element for a `bool` tensor, four for an `f32` one and eight for an `f64` or `c64`
one.

- Pure.
- Example: `to_bytes(new([1.0, 2.0]))` gives `[0, 0, 128, 63, 0, 0, 0, 64]`

#### `save_npy`

```camel
save_npy: (t: T[..], path: string) => void when is_numeric::<T>()
```

Writes a tensor to a NumPy `.npy` file, replacing it.

- With effects: writes a file.
- Failure: fault `RuntimeError` when the file cannot be written.
- Example: `save_npy(zeros([2, 2]), 'x.npy')`

### Module state

#### `num_threads`

```camel
num_threads: () => int
```

The size of the module's worker pool.

- With effects: reads the size of the worker pool.
- Example: `num_threads()`

#### `set_num_threads`

```camel
set_num_threads: (n: int) => void
set_num_threads: (n: i32) => void
```

Sets the size of the module's worker pool; a value below 1 is read as 1.

- With effects: changes the size of the worker pool.
- Example: `set_num_threads(4)`

#### `gemm_backend`

```camel
gemm_backend: () => string
```

The name of the matrix-multiplication kernel the module dispatches to.

- Pure.
- Example: `gemm_backend()`

#### `gemm_threads`

```camel
gemm_threads: () => int
```

The thread count the matrix multiplication had for its most recent call: the tensor-pool
chunks that split a whole-work library product, the worker pool's width for a canonical call,
and 1 inside a region or for a library call inside a batch chunk. The count is what one
product got: `num_threads()` is what the run was given, and this is what one product spent.

- With effects: reads the size of the worker pool.
- Example: `gemm_threads()`

#### `gemm_library_threads`

```camel
gemm_library_threads: () => int
```

The library's own thread count for the most recent call: 1 when a library call ran (each chunk
of a split product is one such call), 0 when the canonical kernel did. `gemm_threads()` is the
pool that split the product; this is what each of its library calls got.

- With effects: reads the thread count of the last library call.
- Example: `gemm_library_threads()`

#### `gemm_library`

```camel
gemm_library: () => string
```

The name of the matrix-multiplication kernel the library path calls: `cblas` in a build with a
CBLAS, otherwise the canonical kernel's name, which is what the path forwards to.

- Pure.
- Example: `gemm_library()`

#### `seed`

```camel
seed: (seed: int) => void
seed: (seed: i32) => void
```

Reseeds the module's random generator, which `random` and `randn` draw from.

- With effects: writes the random generator.
- Example: `seed(42)`

<a id="types"></a>

## `types`: the properties of types

The properties of types that an applicability condition asks about. These are ordinary Camel
functions: each one matches the type it is given with `match type` and returns a constant, so
`func f::<T>(x: T) when is_numeric::<T>()` is applicable exactly where `T` is a number.

`match type` compares a type's identity as well as its shape (design principles 5.5): the
cases below name the types the language spells (`int`, `i32`, `float`, `f32`, `bf16`, `f16`,
`c64`, `c128`, `string`, `bool`), and `case func` is the shape of every function type.

A type is named once: the family predicates (`is_integer`, `is_float`, `is_complex`,
`is_string`, `is_bool`) carry the identity cases, and `is_numeric` and `is_ordered` ask them
instead of listing the types again, so a new integer width is added in one place.

`bf16` and `f16` are floating-point types (design principles 7.3): a tensor
stores an element in one of them, every kernel computes in f32 and rounds once, and the
language itself gives them what it gives `f32`: literals, a written conversion (`bf16(x)`,
`f16(x)`, `x as bf16`), scalar arithmetic and comparison, and arrays of them. They belong to
`is_float` and inherit `is_numeric` and `is_ordered` from it.

#### `is_integer`

```camel
is_integer: () => bool
```

True when `T` is an integer type (`int` is 64-bit, `i32` is 32-bit).

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `is_integer::<int>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_integer::<float>()` gives `false`

#### `is_float`

```camel
is_float: () => bool
```

True when `T` is a floating-point type (`float` is 64-bit, `f32` is 32-bit, `bf16` and
`f16` are the two reduced-precision floating types).

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `is_float::<float>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_float::<bf16>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_float::<int>()` gives `false`

#### `is_complex`

```camel
is_complex: () => bool
```

True when `T` is a complex number (`c64` is 64-bit, `c128` is 128-bit).

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `is_complex::<c64>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_complex::<float>()` gives `false`

#### `is_numeric`

```camel
is_numeric: () => bool
```

True when `T` is a number: an integer, a float or a complex number.

The three families are asked, not listed again: a type spelled in one of them is numeric
without appearing here, so adding an integer width changes `is_integer` alone. The complex
branch is `is_complex`, which is why `c64` is numeric.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `is_numeric::<int>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_numeric::<string>()` gives `false`
- Example: `is_numeric::<c64>()` gives `true`

#### `is_ordered`

```camel
is_ordered: () => bool
```

True when `T` has a total order: the number types, `string` and `bool`.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `is_ordered::<string>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_ordered::<bool>()` gives `true`

#### `is_function`

```camel
is_function: () => bool
```

True when `T` is a function type, whatever its parameters and result.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `is_function::<(x: int) => int>()` gives `true`

#### `is_string`

```camel
is_string: () => bool
```

True when `T` is `string`.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `is_string::<string>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_string::<int>()` gives `false`

#### `is_bool`

```camel
is_bool: () => bool
```

True when `T` is `bool`.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `is_bool::<bool>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_bool::<int>()` gives `false`

#### `is_plain`

```camel
is_plain: () => bool
```

True when `T` is pure data: a number, `bool`, or a struct or tuple whose fields are all pure
data.

Pure data is what a value can be stored as itself: the bytes contain the value and every read of
them is the value again, because no field of the type is a reference. It is the element type an
array is allocated and copied for, the element type `to_bytes` writes and `from_bytes` reads, and
the element type the interchange with other frameworks names. A `string` holds a reference to
its characters, an array holds a reference to its block, and a function, an enum and a tagged
form hold something a copy of the bytes would not carry, so none of them is pure data.

The families are asked here as everywhere else: a number is pure data because `is_numeric` says
so, and a struct or tuple is asked field by field.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `is_plain::<float>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_plain::<bool>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_plain::<{ x: int, y: f32 }>()` gives `true`
- Example: `is_plain::<string>()` gives `false`
- Example: `is_plain::<int[]>()` gives `false`

<a id="array"></a>

## `array`: arrays, sorting and higher-order functions

Array functions and higher-order functions, written in Camel on top of the built-in
operators (map, filter, reduce, range, zip, slice, len) and a few native primitives of this
module (the sorts, argsort, flatten, unique). Every function returns a new value; none changes
its argument.

- The array a function works on is its ordinary argument; a function or a value that
  configures it is a with-argument, as for the built-in `map<f>(xs)` and `slice<a, b>(xs)`,
  so calls chain: `xs->filter<p>->sort_by<key>->take<3>`.
- A result that may not exist is `T?` (`find`, `index_of`, `min`, `max`). Nothing here
  returns an error value, and a wrong argument is a fault of the operator that meets it.
- A function passed to any of these must be pure. The implementation may stop early
  (`find`, `index_of`, `any`, `all`) or, when a fast path is added under `#impl`, apply it to
  several elements at once; the result is the same either way, and no call observes another.
  A function with side effects belongs in `foreach` or `reduce`, which run in order.
- The functions written here are generic: there is one instance per set of element types in
  the whole program, whichever module calls it (one root graph, design principles 10.1).
  `group_by` is not here: it needs the map type.

### Sorting

#### `argsort`

```camel
argsort: (keys: i32[]) => int[]
argsort: (keys: int[]) => int[]
argsort: (keys: f32[]) => int[]
argsort: (keys: float[]) => int[]
argsort: (keys: bool[]) => int[]
argsort: (keys: string[]) => int[]
```

The positions of the keys in ascending order of key; equal keys keep their order (a stable
sort). Keys are numbers, strings (ordered by byte) or bools; NaN keys come last. The
primitive behind `sort_by`.

- A native operator of this module: an opaque node, pure.
- Example: `argsort([30, 10, 20])` gives `[1, 2, 0]`

#### `sort`

```camel
sort: (xs: i32[]) => i32[]
sort: (xs: int[]) => int[]
sort: (xs: f32[]) => f32[]
sort: (xs: float[]) => float[]
```

A sorted copy of xs (quicksort).

- A native operator of this module: an opaque node, pure.
- Example: `sort([3, 1, 2])` gives `[1, 2, 3]`

#### `insert_sort`

```camel
insert_sort: (xs: i32[]) => i32[]
insert_sort: (xs: int[]) => int[]
insert_sort: (xs: f32[]) => f32[]
insert_sort: (xs: float[]) => float[]
```

A sorted copy of xs, by insertion sort.

- A native operator of this module: an opaque node, pure.
- Example: `insert_sort([3, 1, 2])` gives `[1, 2, 3]`

#### `quick_sort`

```camel
quick_sort: (xs: i32[]) => i32[]
quick_sort: (xs: int[]) => int[]
quick_sort: (xs: f32[]) => f32[]
quick_sort: (xs: float[]) => float[]
```

A sorted copy of xs, by quicksort.

- A native operator of this module: an opaque node, pure.
- Example: `quick_sort([3, 1, 2])` gives `[1, 2, 3]`

#### `merge_sort`

```camel
merge_sort: (xs: i32[]) => i32[]
merge_sort: (xs: int[]) => int[]
merge_sort: (xs: f32[]) => f32[]
merge_sort: (xs: float[]) => float[]
```

A sorted copy of xs, by merge sort.

- A native operator of this module: an opaque node, pure.
- Example: `merge_sort([3, 1, 2])` gives `[1, 2, 3]`

#### `merge_sorted_arrays`

```camel
merge_sorted_arrays: (left: i32[], right: i32[]) => i32[]
merge_sorted_arrays: (left: int[], right: int[]) => int[]
merge_sorted_arrays: (left: f32[], right: f32[]) => f32[]
merge_sorted_arrays: (left: float[], right: float[]) => float[]
```

The sorted array made of the elements of two sorted arrays of numbers. The two must hold the
same element type: `T` is one of the four the sorts order, not one per argument.

- A native operator of this module: an opaque node, pure.
- Example: `merge_sorted_arrays([1, 4], [2, 3])` gives `[1, 2, 3, 4]`

### Rearranging

#### `reverse`

```camel
reverse: (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

The elements in reverse order.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `reverse([1, 2, 3])` gives `[3, 2, 1]`

#### `take`

```camel
take: <n: int> (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

The first n elements; all of them when there are fewer, none when n is not positive.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3, 4]->take<2>` gives `[1, 2]`

#### `drop`

```camel
drop: <n: int> (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

The elements after the first n; none when there are fewer, all when n is not positive.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `[1, 2, 3, 4]->drop<1>` gives `[2, 3, 4]`

#### `enumerate`

```camel
enumerate: (xs: T[]) => (int, T)[]
```

Each element with its index.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `enumerate(['a', 'b'])` gives `[(0, 'a'), (1, 'b')]`

#### `flatten`

```camel
flatten: (xss: T[][]) => T[]
```

The elements of the inner arrays, in order. The primitive behind `flat_map`.

- A native operator of this module: an opaque node, pure.
- Example: `flatten([[1, 2], [3]])` gives `[1, 2, 3]`

#### `unique`

```camel
unique: (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

The first occurrence of every value, in order; values are compared as `==` compares them
(a NaN equals nothing, so every NaN is kept).

- A native operator of this module: an opaque node, pure.
- Example: `unique([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])` gives `[3, 1, 2]`

### Searching

#### `index_of`

```camel
index_of: <x: T> (xs: T[]) => int?
```

The index of the first element equal to x, or null.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `[3, 9, 2]->index_of<9> ?? -1` gives `1`

#### `find`

```camel
find: <pred: (x: T) => bool> (xs: T[]) => T?
```

The first element for which pred is true, or null.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `[3, 9, 2]->find<(x: int) => x > 4> ?? -1` gives `9`

#### `any`

```camel
any: <pred: (x: T) => bool> (xs: T[]) => bool
```

True when pred is true for at least one element; false for an empty array.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `[3, 9, 2]->any<(x: int) => x > 4>` gives `true`

#### `all`

```camel
all: <pred: (x: T) => bool> (xs: T[]) => bool
```

True when pred is true for every element; true for an empty array.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `[3, 9, 2]->all<(x: int) => x > 4>` gives `false`

#### `count`

```camel
count: <pred: (x: T) => bool> (xs: T[]) => int
```

The number of elements for which pred is true.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `[3, 9, 2]->count<(x: int) => x > 2>` gives `2`

### Aggregating

#### `sum`

```camel
sum: (xs: T[]) => T when is_numeric::<T>()
```

The sum of the elements, 0 for an empty array.

A floating-point element type accumulates in f64 and rounds once into the element type at the
end: the additions are f64 additions and the result is one conversion of their sum, not a
rounding after every addition (an f32 accumulator rounds at every step and answers
differently). This is the same rule the tensor axis `sum` follows (modules/tensor/kernels/
reduce.cpp: a double accumulator, one rounding when the element is stored), so the two paths
agree bit for bit on the same elements. An integer element type accumulates in itself and
wraps around on overflow, as `+` does on it; a complex element type accumulates in itself as
well, the f64 rule being stated for the floating-point element types.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `sum([1, 2, 3])` gives `6`

#### `min`

```camel
min: (xs: T[]) => T? when is_ordered::<T>()
```

The smallest number (IEEE 754 minimum: a NaN anywhere makes the result NaN, and -0 is below
+0), or null for an empty array.

No accumulator and no accumulation width take part in this fold: it carries an element of T
and combines it with `math::min`, which is IEEE 754 minimum — exactly associative and
commutative (design principles 7.7) — so the order does not change the bits and there is
nothing to round.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `min([3, 9, 2]) ?? 0` gives `2`

#### `max`

```camel
max: (xs: T[]) => T? when is_ordered::<T>()
```

The largest number (IEEE 754 maximum: a NaN anywhere makes the result NaN, and +0 is above
-0), or null for an empty array.

As `min`: the fold carries an element of T, and `math::max` is IEEE 754 maximum, exactly
associative and commutative (design principles 7.7), so no accumulator type enters.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `max([3, 9, 2]) ?? 0` gives `9`

### Transforming

#### `flat_map`

```camel
flat_map: <f: (x: T) => U[]> (xs: T[]) => U[]
```

f applied to every element, the resulting arrays joined in order.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `[1, 2]->flat_map<(x: int) => [x, x * 10]>` gives `[1, 10, 2, 20]`

#### `sort_by`

```camel
sort_by: <key: (x: T) => K> (xs: T[]) => T[]
```

The elements in ascending order of key(x); elements with equal keys keep their order (the
sort is stable, so sorting by one key and then by another works). A key is a number, a string
(ordered by byte) or a bool; NaN keys come last. For a descending order of numbers use the
negated key.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `['pear', 'fig', 'apple']->sort_by<(w: string) => len(w)>` gives `['fig', 'pear', 'apple']`

#### `zip_with`

```camel
zip_with: <f: (a: T, b: U) => V> (xs: T[], ys: U[]) => V[]
```

f(xs[i], ys[i]) for every i.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Failure: fault `InvalidArgument` (of zip) when the two arrays differ in length.
- Example: `zip_with<(a: int, b: int) => a + b>([1, 2], [10, 20])` gives `[11, 22]`

<a id="stream"></a>

## `stream`: producing and consuming streams

Streams, written in Camel. A stream's value is its step function together with its state (design
principles 5.4, and the reading of 2026-10-26): `T..` is an ordinary function value of the
signature `() => (T, T..)?`, one call is one pull, and a pull answers the next element together
with the rest of the stream -- `null` when the stream is over. So the producers here are
ordinary functions that return such a closure, and the consumer is `for x in s`, which the
compiler expands on the graph into the `while` it already has (language reference 7.3.2). No
part of this module needs a new node kind, and none of it runs anything by itself: pulling is
what runs, one element at a time.

- `unfold(state, step)` is the smallest producer: a state and a step that answers the next
  element with the state after it, or `null` when the stream is over. A `yield` generator
  compiles to the same kind of value, and one written `#op` source can hand one out too.
- `tee(s, n)` is the one way to read one stream from two places: it reads `s` once and gives two
  streams, each of which is read once, and both see the same elements.
- A stream is a value and is pure, so pulling the same stream value twice answers the same
  element; the rest a pull hands out is what threads the stream, and the consumer passes it on.
  One stream value has one consumer per execution path (design principles 5.4).

### Producing

#### `unfold`

```camel
unfold: (state: S, step: (state: S) => (T, S)?) => T..
```

The stream of what `step` answers from `state` on: one element with the state after it, or
`null` when there is nothing more. The first round of `for x in s` over it is `step(state)`,
and every later round is a pull of the rest, so the states are threaded rather than repeated.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example: `loop acc = 0 for x in unfold(3, (n: int) => if n > 0 then (n, n - 1) else null) do acc + x` gives `6`

### Splitting

#### `tee`

```camel
tee: (s: T.., n: int = 8) => (T.., T..)
```

Two streams over the elements of `s` (design principles 5.4), each read once, both seeing the
same elements in the same order. `s` is read once: the first side to need an element the buffer
does not hold pulls it, and the other side finds it there. `n` is a hint -- the width the
buffer is expected to have -- and is clamped to the implementation's cap.
The result is a tuple, and taking it apart is what consumes the two streams; the streams
themselves are values like any other, so a `tee` of one of them is another `tee`.

- Written in Camel: a subgraph, pure when the functions passed to it are.
- Example (a fragment, not compiled): `let (left, right) = tee(unfold(3, (n: int) => if n > 0 then (n, n - 1) else null), 2)`
